Endurance Expedition [6121]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Shackleton Pitch

It’s the centenary of Ernest Shackleton death - will the SAS Aghulhas find the wreck of his ship the Endurance in icy waters.

It’s the stuff of adventurer’s dreams. Endurance 22 is an expedition to find the sunken wreck of the Endurance that may lie 10 000m under sea.

Sir Ernest Henry Shackleton (15 February 1874 – 5 January 1922) was an Irish explorer who led three British expeditions to the Antarctic. He was one of the main figures that has featured in what is referred to as the heroic age of Antarctic Expeditions.

Endurance was one of two ships used by the imperial Trans-Antarctic expedition, led by Ernest Shackleton, which hoped to complete the first land crossing of the Antarctic.
The 144-foot-long, three-masted schooner was sturdily built for expeditions during polar winters but became stuck in pack ice on the Weddell Sea while attempting to land at Vahsel Bay on January 18, 1915.
The vessel and its 28-man crew remained stuck in the pack ice for many months until the ship was steadily crushed by the ice following a huge drop in temperatures in late October. The ship finally sank on November 21, 1915, prompting Shackleton and his crew to make their way across the ice to Elephant Island.
The Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust is now set to launch the Endurance22 expedition on February 5. The expedition was announced on January 5 to mark the 100th-anniversary of Shackleton's death.

Below is an article from the New York Times.

The hunt is on for Endurance, Ernest Shackleton’s ship that sits 10,000 feet below the icy Weddell Sea in Antarctica.
After an 11-day voyage aboard the SAS Aghulas, South African icebreaker, the expedition, known as Endurance22, began searching for the wreck this week.
Captained by Knowledge Bengu it is the second expedition that he has captained to search for the Endurance. He will grant us an interview. Underwater drones equipped with cameras, sonar and lasers have been scanning 100 square miles of seafloor looking for the remains of the 144-foot wooden ship, which sank in 1915 after being crushed in ice.
Mensun Bound, the expedition’s director of exploration, said in an email that after a few technical glitches, the submersibles were functioning well, carrying out several dives each day. Images show that the seafloor is flat and consists of fine sediment and small rocks. “It should be possible to identify quickly any wreckage,” he said.
The expedition, financed at a cost of more than $10 million by an anonymous donor, has about a week left before the icebreaker, Agulhas II, must head back to Cape Town. (We can get interview with Expedition Director)
But the expedition is not only looking for one of the most celebrated wrecks that remain to be found, a ship with a revered place in the history of Antarctic exploration. On board are researchers with a more forward-looking goal: They are studying the Weddell Sea pack ice, looking for signs that it is changing as the world warms as a result of human-cause emissions of greenhouse gases. (I can find a UCT Climate Expert to comment here if we go with two programmes? If we get to speak to their climatologist as well that would be wonderful)
Two helicopters aboard the ship have been used to ferry these scientists to ice floes, where ice cores are drilled for later laboratory analysis. (These are piloted by South Africans and I have secured interviews here and with the owner of the helicopter company Shaun Roseveare who has been on both expeditions and sponsored helicopters. The helicopters have been pivotal in getting the submarines further in land to speed up the expedition.)
Endurance was lost while transporting Shackleton and his crew of 27 to Antarctica for what was to have been an attempt to be the first to cross the continent on foot. The sinking, which came months after the ship first became trapped in pack ice, dashed those hopes but resulted in one of the greatest tales of survival in the face of great adversity. Shackleton led some of his men on an epic small-boat voyage to the island of South Georgia, a journey of 800 miles, from where he organized the rescue of the entire crew. He returned to Britain a hero.

(There is wonderful black and white footage of The Shackleton’s main mask cracking in the ice. Will make enquiries where to get this and other stock.)
As Shackleton learned first hand, the Weddell is notorious for having thick, years-old ice, a function of the sea’s circular current. But the ice en route to the search site was not too bad, said John Shears, the expedition leader. “Our transit was much quicker than expected because of the light ice conditions, with plenty of open water leads available for the ship to maneuver through,” he said.
The ice at the search area has also not presented any obstacles, Mr. Bound said. It is thin enough that the icebreaker’s propeller wash creates enough open water to launch the submersibles. He said that while the search was in its early stages, the team was making good progress covering the search area.
Endurance’s captain, Frank Worsley, was able to use basic navigational tools to determine the ship’s location when it finally sank. But Worsley’s timepiece, which he used to make noontime sightings of the sun, was off by about 10 minutes. Through analyses of that and other potential errors, as well as modeling of possible drift, a 7 mile by 14 mile search area was established.

If the remains of the ship are found, the submersibles will take videos and photographs and make laser scans of the wreckage, which will very likely be the basis for museum exhibits and educational materials. But the site, which is classified as a historic monument, will not be disturbed.

Endurance Edit 6 Final Script

Endurance Script 6
V/O
For decades historians have been plotting the search for Antarctic explorer Sir Henry Spencer Shackleton’s wreck.
Eerily preserved in its icy grave, this is Endurance…last seen over a century ago when it was crushed by ice. It is an untouched relic of Shackleton’s ill-fated attempt to cross the South Pole - on foot - in 1914.
And now, a centenary after Shackleton’s death, the wreck has finally been discovered by an international expedition with a large South African contingent on board.
Captain Knowledge Bhengu, who grew up in Umlazi in Durban skippers the Agulhas II… it’s South Africa’s ice-breaking polar supply and research ship that was commissioned to search for the wreck.
He was asleep when the news broke. His first officer woke him up.
Knowledge Bengu
“He said Captain Knowledge Bhengu I am sorry to disturb you we have found the Endurance, I was in my deepest sleep. I was like no ways, I jumped up. I saw it laying there in its pristine state, looking beautiful. It was like a huge relief off my shoulders. Because I understand what this means, this is history of 107 years.”
V/O
Mounting an expedition like this, in the formidable Antarctic continent is fraught with difficulties. Temperatures average minus 49 degrees Celcius.
https://www.climatestotravel.com/climate/antarctica
Rob Caskie
“At the turn of the last century, the interior of Antarctica and 90 degrees south, the South Pole was about as distant to the human mind as the surface of the moon.”
V/O
Storyteller Rob Caskie has been leading tours to Antarctica for a decade.
The first to reach the South Pole, triumphantly, on the 14th of December 1911, was Roald Amundsen’s Norwegian team. Thirty four days later Britain’s Captain Robert Falcon Scott also made it, only to discover he’d been pipped to the post. Scott and his team died tragically while returning to base camp.
Rob
“Particularly, I'm interested in human beings when the chips are down, when things go wrong. And the Shackleton story, of course, and the Robert Falcon Scott story lend themselves beautifully to sagas of human endeavour, human triumph and indeed human tragedy.”
V/O
Not to be outdone, Shackleton felt that crossing Antarctica would be the last great prize left for humankind after the South Pole had been reached.
His Endurance set sail in 1914 with a crew of 27 men.
Bongani Link
“It was the age of heroes, the race to the South Pole, who would be first. Over 100 years ago, Shackleton and his crew did not quite make it.”
V/O
Reportedly the pack ice that year was the worst in living memory.
Rob
“So Shackleton had to push the heavily laden endurance down through the pack ice, and got right down to 43 miles from land mid-January 1915. When the wind turned, the temperature plummeted and the sea froze, trapping their ship like an almond in a slab of chocolate.”
V/O
The ship snapped like a twig underneath the immense pressure of the ice. Shackleton told his crew “What the ice gets, the ice keeps.” After living in these extreme conditions for 10 months, they abandoned ship.
On the 27th October 1915 Shackleton wrote this in his diary.
ACTOR Voice
“The end came at last about 5pm - she was doomed, no ship built by human hands could have withstood the strain.”
V/O
The Endurance sank in November 1915. For five months the crew pressed on north and set up camp on Elephant Island…a gruelling trip of about 400km with minimal protection against the inhospitable elements.
Captain Knowledge Bhengu
“Men in those days were made out of steel and ships made out of wood. You know and today, we more like made out of wood and ships made out of steel.”




V/O
Technology has changed the face of exploration. The Augulhas is made with a double reinforced steel hull that cuts through ice like butter.
Bongani
“How thick does the ice get?”
KB
“The ship is designed to go through 1m thick ice at 5 knots, that about 9 kmph continuously. But in most case we have broken through plus minus 5 m of ice when we are backing and ramming.”
Bongani Link
“The Agulhas II is about as sophisticated as it gets. Underneath that dome is a satellite navigation system, there are at least 3 on board, there is internet available here, telephones, if anything goes wrong, they can alert someone and let them know they are in trouble. Shackleton and his Endurance team had none of that.”
V/O
On reaching Elephant Island, he took a boat and 5 crew members to get help from a whaling station - over a thousand kilometers away.
Rob Caskie
“When the ship was first beset, he said to his dear friend, Wild if I am not back in 3 months, you consider us dead and make the best plan you can for the men.”
Shaun Roseveare
“I can imagine it must have been extremely frightening for them. The Augulhas II also had the luxury of helicopters on board as well as other ships in the area that could have come to their rescue. 100 years ago it must have been extremely frightening for Shackleton.”
V/O
Shaun Roseveare owns the company that supplied the expedition choppers.
Bongani
“What did it feel like to be part of this historic mission?”
Shaun
“It’s a once in a life time opportunity, something for all of us to be proud of. About 70% of the crew on the ship were all South Africans.”

V/O
Charlie Tait was one of the pilots.
Bongani
“What is it like to fly in Antarctica?”
Charlie
“It’s pretty awesome , fantastic scenery but Antarctica is as dangerous as it is beautiful.”
V/O
With ice as far as the eye can see, finding the wreck seemed an impossible task.
Bongani
“Where did you know where to look?”

Knowledge
“Shackleton’s navigator was a very skilled navigator and he worked out the sinking location using the sextant.”

V/O
(A sextant… and the equipment on board Agulhas II are poles apart. )

The Endurance expedition assembled world-leading marine archaeologists and sea-ice scientists with advanced underwater technology to locate the wreck. A specially-built hybrid Autonomous Underwater Vehicle was fitted with High-Definition cameras to scan the ocean floor at exceptionally great depths.
This was the second attempt to discover the wreck. The international crew included British polar geographer Dr John Shears as expedition leader… and Mensun Bound, a maritime archaeologist as Director of Exploration. Scanning for a tiny wreck in a vast, deep, inky ocean took hundreds of hours.

Mesun
“You are absolutely sick with nerves and then we were getting down the line, getting down the line not finding it and finally the last few days and there was nothing, then boof all of a sudden it just erupts in your face.”

John
“I was stunned, absolutely stunned, because the wreck is in incredible condition , there is virtually nothing living on it at all, it is as if it sunk only yesterday.”

Bongani Link
“The wreck of the Endurance was found at a depth of 3000m.That may just seem like a number but signal hill behind me is 2.6 km away from where I am standing so that means the Endurance was found at a depth longer than from here to over there.”

John
“The wreck is protected under the Antarctic Treaty as an historic site there won’t be anything taken off it at all it will be left completely alone.”

V/O
What makes Shackleton a hero is not an Antarctic record, but that he sacrificed everything to get the men under his command to safety. He came back 4 months later on a rescue ship and not one his crew lost their lives.

B
“What did it mean for you to be the Captain of the ship that found the Endurance?”

KB
“World history for South Africa for myself for the company, and when the world is watching, they know that we have skilled sea farers that capability to make it to the world stage.”

Bongani
“What did it feel like to be a part of this historic mission?”
Charlie
“Absolutely fantastic, electrifying, there was a feeling of great euphoria on the ship.”
Bongani
“Mission A
accomplished”

Charlie
“Mission Accomplished”



Promo 1
V/O
This is the mighty Endurance … one of the world’s most pristinely preserved shipwrecks in history…
V/O
And this is the Agulhas II - South Africa’s toughest ice breaker … together, it’s the story of two legends

Promo 2
V/O

The Agulhas II - South Africa’s most powerful ice-breaker - has come home after a victorious expedition in the Antarctic.

UPSOUND: They woke me up ….

V/O

The historic wreckage of Sir Henry Ernest Shackleton’s Endurance was located by the mighty Algulhas II.

Promo 3

V/O

For over century, it lay on the ocean floor… in the deep icy waters of the Antarctic … now the Agulhas II, South African crew alongside a team of international researchers, have found the historic wreckage of Sir Henry Ernest Shackleton’s mighty Endurance.

For five months the crew pressed on north and set up camp on Elephant Island…a gruelling trip of about 400km with minimal protection against the inhospitable elements. Captain Knowledge Bhengu “Men in those days were made out of steel and ships made out of wood. You know and today, we more like made out of wood and ships made out of steel.” V/O Technology has changed the face of exploration. The Augulhas is made with a double reinforced steel hull that cuts through ice like butter. Bongani “How thick does the ice get?” KB “The ship is designed to go through 1m thick ice at 5 knots, that about 9 kmph continuously. But in most case we have broken through plus minus 5 m of ice when we are backing and ramming.” Bongani Link “The Agulhas II is about as sophisticated as it gets. Underneath that dome is a satellite navigation system, there are at least 3 on board, there is internet available here, telephones, if anything goes wrong, they can alert someone and let them know they are in trouble. Shackleton and his Endurance team had none of that.” V/O On reaching Elephant Island, he took a boat and 5 crew members to get help from a whaling station - over a thousand kilometers away. Rob Caskie “When the ship was first beset, he said to his dear friend, Wild if I am not back in 3 months, you consider us dead and make the best plan you can for the men.” Shaun Roseveare “I can imagine it must have been extremely frightening for them. The Augulhas II also had the luxury of helicopters on board as well as other ships in the area that could have come to their rescue. 100 years ago it must have been extremely frightening for Shackleton.” V/O Shaun Roseveare owns the company that supplied the expedition choppers. Bongani “What did it feel like to be part of this historic mission?” Shaun “It’s a once in a life time opportunity, something for all of us to be proud of. About 70% of the crew on the ship were all South Africans.” V/O Charlie Tait was one of the pilots. Bongani “What is it like to fly in Antarctica?” Charlie “It’s pretty awesome , fantastic scenery but Antarctica is as dangerous as it is beautiful.” V/O With ice as far as the eye can see, finding the wreck seemed an impossible task. Bongani “Where did you know where to look?” Knowledge “Shackleton’s navigator was a very skilled navigator and he worked out the sinking location using the sextant.” V/O (A sextant… and the equipment on board Agulhas II are poles apart. ) The Endurance expedition assembled world-leading marine archaeologists and sea-ice scientists with advanced underwater technology to locate the wreck. A specially-built hybrid Autonomous Underwater Vehicle was fitted with High-Definition cameras to scan the ocean floor at exceptionally great depths. This was the second attempt to discover the wreck. The international crew included British polar geographer Dr John Shears as expedition leader… and Mensun Bound, a maritime archaeologist as Director of Exploration. Scanning for a tiny wreck in a vast, deep, inky ocean took hundreds of hours. Mesun “You are absolutely sick with nerves and then we were getting down the line, getting down the line not finding it and finally the last few days and there was nothing, then boof all of a sudden it just erupts in your face.” John “I was stunned, absolutely stunned, because the wreck is in incredible condition , there is virtually nothing living on it at all, it is as if it sunk only yesterday.” Bongani Link “The wreck of the Endurance was found at a depth of 3000m.That may just seem like a number but signal hill behind me is 2.6 km away from where I am standing so that means the Endurance was found at a depth longer than from here to over there.” John “The wreck is protected under the Antarctic Treaty as an historic site there won’t be anything taken off it at all it will be left completely alone.” V/O What makes Shackleton a hero is not an Antarctic record, but that he sacrificed everything to get the men under his command to safety. He came back 4 months later on a rescue ship and not one his crew lost their lives. B “What did it mean for you to be the Captain of the ship that found the Endurance?” KB “World history for South Africa for myself for the company, and when the world is watching, they know that we have skilled sea farers that capability to make it to the world stage.” Bongani “What did it feel like to be a part of this historic mission?” Charlie “Absolutely fantastic, electrifying, there was a feeling of great euphoria on the ship.” Bongani “Mission A accomplished” Charlie “Mission Accomplished” Promo 1 V/O This is the mighty Endurance … one of the world’s most pristinely preserved shipwrecks in history… V/O And this is the Agulhas II - South Africa’s toughest ice breaker … together, it’s the story of two legends Promo 2 V/O The Agulhas II - South Africa’s most powerful ice-breaker - has come home after a victorious expedition in the Antarctic. UPSOUND: They woke me up …. V/O The historic wreckage of Sir Henry Ernest Shackleton’s Endurance was located by the mighty Algulhas II. Promo 3 V/O For over century, it lay on the ocean floor… in the deep icy waters of the Antarctic … now the Agulhas II, South African crew alongside a team of international researchers, have found the historic wreckage of Sir Henry Ernest Shackleton’s mighty Endurance.

metadata.Further information: Shackleton Pitch It’s the centenary of Ernest Shackleton death - will the SAS Aghulhas find the wreck of his ship the Endurance in icy waters. It’s the stuff of adventurer’s dreams. Endurance 22 is an expedition to find the sunken wreck of the Endurance that may lie 10 000m under sea. Sir Ernest Henry Shackleton (15 February 1874 – 5 January 1922) was an Irish explorer who led three British expeditions to the Antarctic. He was one of the main figures that has featured in what is referred to as the heroic age of Antarctic Expeditions. Endurance was one of two ships used by the imperial Trans-Antarctic expedition, led by Ernest Shackleton, which hoped to complete the first land crossing of the Antarctic. The 144-foot-long, three-masted schooner was sturdily built for expeditions during polar winters but became stuck in pack ice on the Weddell Sea while attempting to land at Vahsel Bay on January 18, 1915. The vessel and its 28-man crew remained stuck in the pack ice for many months until the ship was steadily crushed by the ice following a huge drop in temperatures in late October. The ship finally sank on November 21, 1915, prompting Shackleton and his crew to make their way across the ice to Elephant Island. The Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust is now set to launch the Endurance22 expedition on February 5. The expedition was announced on January 5 to mark the 100th-anniversary of Shackleton's death. Below is an article from the New York Times. The hunt is on for Endurance, Ernest Shackleton’s ship that sits 10,000 feet below the icy Weddell Sea in Antarctica. After an 11-day voyage aboard the SAS Aghulas, South African icebreaker, the expedition, known as Endurance22, began searching for the wreck this week. Captained by Knowledge Bengu it is the second expedition that he has captained to search for the Endurance. He will grant us an interview. Underwater drones equipped with cameras, sonar and lasers have been scanning 100 square miles of seafloor looking for the remains of the 144-foot wooden ship, which sank in 1915 after being crushed in ice. Mensun Bound, the expedition’s director of exploration, said in an email that after a few technical glitches, the submersibles were functioning well, carrying out several dives each day. Images show that the seafloor is flat and consists of fine sediment and small rocks. “It should be possible to identify quickly any wreckage,” he said. The expedition, financed at a cost of more than $10 million by an anonymous donor, has about a week left before the icebreaker, Agulhas II, must head back to Cape Town. (We can get interview with Expedition Director) But the expedition is not only looking for one of the most celebrated wrecks that remain to be found, a ship with a revered place in the history of Antarctic exploration. On board are researchers with a more forward-looking goal: They are studying the Weddell Sea pack ice, looking for signs that it is changing as the world warms as a result of human-cause emissions of greenhouse gases. (I can find a UCT Climate Expert to comment here if we go with two programmes? If we get to speak to their climatologist as well that would be wonderful) Two helicopters aboard the ship have been used to ferry these scientists to ice floes, where ice cores are drilled for later laboratory analysis. (These are piloted by South Africans and I have secured interviews here and with the owner of the helicopter company Shaun Roseveare who has been on both expeditions and sponsored helicopters. The helicopters have been pivotal in getting the submarines further in land to speed up the expedition.) Endurance was lost while transporting Shackleton and his crew of 27 to Antarctica for what was to have been an attempt to be the first to cross the continent on foot. The sinking, which came months after the ship first became trapped in pack ice, dashed those hopes but resulted in one of the greatest tales of survival in the face of great adversity. Shackleton led some of his men on an epic small-boat voyage to the island of South Georgia, a journey of 800 miles, from where he organized the rescue of the entire crew. He returned to Britain a hero. (There is wonderful black and white footage of The Shackleton’s main mask cracking in the ice. Will make enquiries where to get this and other stock.) As Shackleton learned first hand, the Weddell is notorious for having thick, years-old ice, a function of the sea’s circular current. But the ice en route to the search site was not too bad, said John Shears, the expedition leader. “Our transit was much quicker than expected because of the light ice conditions, with plenty of open water leads available for the ship to maneuver through,” he said. The ice at the search area has also not presented any obstacles, Mr. Bound said. It is thin enough that the icebreaker’s propeller wash creates enough open water to launch the submersibles. He said that while the search was in its early stages, the team was making good progress covering the search area. Endurance’s captain, Frank Worsley, was able to use basic navigational tools to determine the ship’s location when it finally sank. But Worsley’s timepiece, which he used to make noontime sightings of the sun, was off by about 10 minutes. Through analyses of that and other potential errors, as well as modeling of possible drift, a 7 mile by 14 mile search area was established. If the remains of the ship are found, the submersibles will take videos and photographs and make laser scans of the wreckage, which will very likely be the basis for museum exhibits and educational materials. But the site, which is classified as a historic monument, will not be disturbed.
